title: KEA's QR-code facial recognition app exposes a woman trying to enter a Bengaluru CET hall on another candidate's forged admit card
summary: KEA's facial recognition app flagged a woman with a forged CET admit card in Bengaluru on 17 April 2025; she fled before writing the paper.
account: On Thursday 17 April 2025 a woman calling herself Tuba Fathima Jameel tried to enter the CET-2025 mathematics paper. The center was Silver Valley Public PU College in Malleswaram, Bengaluru. She had spent nearly an hour in the restroom. Her admit card carried her own pasted photograph and an altered name. It bore the hall ticket number and QR code of a genuine candidate, Tabu Naz. Staff scanned the code and captured her photo with the new Karnataka Examinations Authority (KEA) facial recognition app. It reported that she was not the candidate on record. She fled before the principal was told. KEA executive director H. Prasanna ordered a report with video footage and said legal action would follow.
purpose: KEA built the app to verify candidates at the hall entrance and prevent impersonation. It scans the admit card's QR code and matches a live photograph against the photo submitted at registration. Exposing this impersonator was exactly that purpose.
system: Karnataka Examinations Authority QR code-based facial recognition app (CET-2025 candidate verification)
developer: Karnataka Examinations Authority (The Hindu and ETV Bharat: 'developed by KEA'; no vendor named)

ratings.reason: KEA stopped a forged-entry attempt in the app's first state-wide run. The Hindu reports that all verifications ran without technical glitches on the second day. The benefit to the authority is a working integrity control across 3,30,808 registrants, demonstrated on one case.

Genuine CET-2025 candidates: one person who was not the candidate on record was kept out of a competition for seats among 3.3 lakh registrants. It is a small benefit spread across the cohort. The sources do not say what she meant to gain.

ai_role.statement: The app did the detecting. Staff scanned the admit card's QR code and captured the woman's photo. It flagged a mismatch with the photo on record (New Indian Express). It “revealed that she was not the genuine candidate” (The Hindu). The Hindu and the Times of India both report the forged card's contents. It carried her own photograph with the genuine candidate's hall ticket number and QR code. Comparing the card with her face would therefore not have exposed her. The flag depended on the app's match against the registered photograph. Staff then acted, but she fled before the principal was told. No arrest or sanction is attributable to the system. KEA's probe and the promised legal action were still pending in every report.

produced_by: Admit cards printed with a QR code that resolves to the candidate's registered record and photograph. A photo pasted over the card therefore does not change what the app compares against.
A live photograph taken at the hall door and matched by the app against the registered photo before entry. This ran at every center rather than the earlier pilot subset.
Center staff instructed to act on a mismatch and escalate to the principal and KEA. Video coverage of the entrance that KEA could call for afterwards.
must_hold: The registered photograph must be of the genuine candidate. The control fails if the fraud is committed at registration rather than at the door.
Verification must be completed before the candidate is admitted. This depends on staffing and app reliability at scale. KEA reported no glitches this time.
A flagged person must be detained or identified on the spot. Here she fled, so the deterrent rests on the probe and the video footage rather than on an arrest.

headline: KEA's facial recognition app exposes a forged CET admit card

later.note: A year later KEA announced that facial recognition and QR-code verification would again be done for every candidate at K-CET 2026 on 23-24 April 2026.
later.quote: In order to avoid impersonation of candidates, facial recognition and QR code verification will be done for every candidate.

revisions.change: Record drafted from the OECD Monitor entry and the cited sources. Filed as specific harm prevented, as the classifier proposed: the harm was specific (entry to the mathematics paper under a genuine candidate's hall ticket number) and the supporting evidence is that the forged card carried the impersonator's own photograph, so the app's match against the registered photo, not a visual check, produced the flag, and she left without writing the paper. Every account traces to a statement by KEA executive director H. Prasanna; KEA both built and ran the app, and no police record, court filing or outcome of the promised legal action was found. The Hindu says the catch came on the app's second day, the Times of India on its third (counting the Kannada paper of 15 April). Dated to the attempt, Thursday 17 April 2025; the Monitor's ID date (14 April) is the Times of India preview of the new security norms. The Monitor spells the name “Tuba Fatima Jameel” after ETV Bharat; The Hindu, the Times of India and the New Indian Express print “Tuba Fathima Jameel”, and the genuine candidate appears as “Tabu Naz” (Hindu, TOI, NIE) and “Tabu Naaz” (ETV). Udayavani's page sat behind a bot check and was not read.
